title: Post-Quantum Cryptography in Spring Boot: Four Patterns You Can Ship This Sprint
gist: A retail-banking case study argues that post-quantum cryptography migration is already urgent because of Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later attacks, that JDK 24's native ML-KEM/ML-DSA support removes the excuse to wait, and that the real blocker to production PQC is key management (KMS/Vault) rather than the cryptography itself -- with a concrete risk-prioritized rollout sequence for Spring Boot banking systems.

themes.theme: The urgency case: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later

insights.claim: Adversaries are already intercepting and storing encrypted TLS traffic today so they can decrypt it later once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists, meaning customer SSNs, transaction records, and KYC documents flowing between services right now are already at risk even though no quantum computer can break RSA-2048 yet.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: This reframes PQC migration from a future compliance task into a present-day data-confidentiality problem for any organization handling long-lived sensitive data over TLS -- waiting for a cloud provider to add PQC TLS is not a safe default.
insights.quote: Someone is storing your RSA-wrapped TLS sessions right now to decrypt later, so any customer SSNs, transaction records, and Know Your Customer (KYC) documents flowing between your services today are already at risk.

insights.claim: A quantum computer running Shor's Algorithm can factor large numbers and solve discrete logarithms in polynomial time, breaking both RSA and ECDSA; IBM, Google, and national labs already operate working quantum processors, though none yet at the scale needed to break RSA-2048, with most experts putting that crossover between 2030 and 2035.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Gives investors and security planners a rough timeline (2030-2035) for when RSA/ECDSA-protected data becomes actually decryptable, anchoring urgency for anything with a multi-year confidentiality requirement.

insights.claim: A loan agreement signed with RSA today will have a forgeable signature around 2035, and because banks archive loan agreements, contracts, and audit trails for seven to thirty years, this creates a legal liability that cannot be fixed retroactively by re-signing archived documents after the fact.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Long-lived signed documents carry a distinct, time-bound legal risk separate from data confidentiality -- financial and legal institutions with multi-decade document retention face a hard deadline to migrate signing infrastructure, not just encryption.
insights.locator: Start your PQC migration with the data that lives the longest

themes.theme: Prioritization framework: migrate by data lifetime, not familiarity

insights.claim: The author argues PQC migration should start with the data that lives longest rather than the authorization layer that feels most familiar, because short-lived customer session tokens (roughly 15-minute expiry) are low risk -- they're worthless before anyone could crack them -- while OAuth2 tokens and service-account credentials for core banking, fraud detection, and regulatory reporting often live for months or years and are exactly what Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later attacks target.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Gives security teams at any organization (not just banks) a concrete, generalizable prioritization rule for PQC rollout order: rank assets by data/credential lifetime, not by which layer feels most urgent to engineers.

insights.claim: The recommended immediate rollout order is: get AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault in place for Kyber key management first, then add Kyber+AES-256-GCM payload encryption to the two or three service flows carrying the most sensitive data, then switch loan-agreement and regulatory document signing to Dilithium -- with payload encryption across the rest of the service mesh, ORM field-encryption helpers, CI/CD artifact signing, and PQC-aware OAuth2 token signing deferred to the following six to eighteen months.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: A concrete, sequenced migration roadmap that security and platform teams can adopt directly, and a signal of near-term demand for KMS/Vault-style key-management services tied specifically to PQC compliance projects.

themes.theme: Key management, not cryptography, is the real blocker

insights.claim: Encrypting a database field with a Kyber key is not the hard part; the hard part is ensuring the private key never lives in the JVM heap, because a single server restart or heap dump can permanently undo every encrypted row in the database if there's no persistent, external key store.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: This is the article's central operational thesis: PQC field-level encryption that looks complete in a demo is not production-safe without external key management -- a warning for any team about to ship 'working' PQC code without KMS integration.
insights.quote: Encrypting a database field with a Kyber key is not the hard part; rather, the hard part is making sure that key does not live in your JVM heap, because one server restart or one heap dump undoes every encrypted row in your database.

insights.claim: Without routing Kyber key operations through AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault, field-level encryption has three problems that will fail a banking security audit: no persistent key store means a restart makes all encrypted records unreadable, a heap dump exposes the master private key for every encrypted record, and there is no key rotation, which GLBA, PCI-DSS, and SOC 2 all explicitly require.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Names the specific compliance frameworks (GLBA, PCI-DSS, SOC 2) that make naive key handling a hard audit failure, not just a theoretical risk -- directly relevant to any regulated-industry engineering team building PQC encryption.
insights.quote: Without it, what you have is a working proof of concept, not a deployable system.
insights.locator: The Key Management Problem That Blocks Field-Level Encryption

insights.claim: Of the four PQC patterns covered, document and artifact signing with Dilithium is the closest to production-ready because it does not depend on KMS being in place first and has a legal/compliance urgency concrete enough to win sign-off from legal and compliance teams.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Identifies document signing as the lowest-friction, highest-ROI first PQC deployment for regulated enterprises -- a near-term, shippable action item distinct from the harder encryption/key-management work.
insights.locator: Of the four patterns in this article

themes.theme: Concrete patterns, overhead, and vendor/platform choices

insights.claim: If a team is already on JDK 24, ML-KEM and ML-DSA are available through the standard Java Cryptography Extension with no external library required (via JEP 496 and JEP 497), meaning the JDK 24 upgrade teams were likely already planning also unblocks the entire PQC migration; Bouncy Castle remains necessary for JDK 11/17 shops.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Ties PQC migration timing directly to routine JDK upgrade cycles, meaning enterprises already planning a JDK 24 move get PQC readiness essentially for free -- an underappreciated argument for accelerating JDK upgrades, and a headwind for third-party PQC crypto library vendors like Bouncy Castle once JDK 24 adoption rises.
insights.quote: The JDK upgrade (JDK 24) you were probably already planning also unblocks your entire post-quantum cryptography (PQC) migration.

insights.claim: The recommended architecture pattern is dual-layer: encrypt HTTP payloads with Kyber+AES-256-GCM independent of TLS, because in typical banking infrastructure TLS is terminated at API gateways, service meshes, and internal load balancers, leaving the actual microservice-to-microservice hop unencrypted inside the perimeter.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Highlights a common but under-discussed enterprise security gap -- internal TLS termination -- that application-layer PQC encryption specifically addresses, independent of whatever the cloud provider does with PQC TLS.

insights.claim: Kyber-768 public keys are around 1,184 bytes (fine in an HTTP body but not headers) and Dilithium-3 signatures are around 3,300 bytes versus 256 bytes for RS256, large enough to break JWT claim size limits, ISO 20022 message envelope limits, or API gateway request size limits if not accounted for.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: A concrete, easy-to-miss operational cost of PQC adoption: message size roughly 13x larger for signatures, which teams must budget into network, gateway, and message-format configuration before rollout.

insights.claim: Full Spring Security integration for the OAuth2 flow with Dilithium token signing is still in progress in the open-source ecosystem, so quantum-safe service-account token signing should be treated as near-term planned work rather than something shippable today.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Flags an open-source tooling gap: enterprise Spring shops cannot yet fully close the highest-priority OAuth2/service-account HNDL exposure without custom integration work, a near-term opportunity for the Spring ecosystem or PQC tooling vendors.

insights.claim: PQC support natively in TLS 1.3 itself depends on JEP 527 landing in the upcoming JDK 27 release and on cloud providers supporting the new cipher suites, reinforcing that waiting for the platform layer to add PQC TLS is not a viable near-term migration plan.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Sets an approximate timeline dependency (JDK 27 plus cloud provider adoption) for when transport-layer PQC becomes available, reinforcing why application-layer patterns are needed as a stopgap now.
insights.locator: Make these changes In the next six to eighteen months

insights.claim: Signing every JAR deployed into banking infrastructure with Dilithium via the CI/CD build pipeline, and verifying that signature before any kubectl apply, catches supply-chain injection between the artifact registry and production -- an attack surface standard TLS cannot detect because it occurs inside the registry boundary.
insights.speaker: Pankaj Sharma
insights.so_what: Extends PQC signing beyond data protection into software supply-chain security, an increasingly scrutinized risk area for regulated industries and a use case that doesn't require the harder key-management workstream.
